content: 1. The risk ratio (RR) could not be estimated due to a numerator of zero. 2. The GRADE assessment for social media-based interventions was conducted by a team of authors, including Anjuli Wagner, Irene Njuguna, Jaclyn Escudero, Rachael Burke, Chris Obermeyer, Jill Neary, Bastien Mollo, Michelle Bulterys, Ruchi Tiwari, Hannah Han, Ngozi Kalu, Dorothy Mangale, Wenwen Jiang, Alison Drake, David Katz, Magdalena Barr-DiChiara, Muhammad S. Jamil, Rachel Baggaley, Nandi Siegfried, and Cheryl Johnson. 3. The primary question addressed was whether social media-based interventions are effective in increasing the uptake of HIV testing and subsequent linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. 4. The certainty of evidence for the uptake of HIV testing was rated as very low, with social media interventions showing an improvement in uptake (64% vs. 42%), but no denominators were reported. 5. Linkage to care among individuals testing positive for HIV was not reported. 6. The number of new HIV-positive diagnoses was not reported. 7. The yield of HIV testing services (HTS) was not reported. 8. Viral load outcomes among individuals testing positive were not reported. 9. Linkage to prevention services was not reported. 10. The time to retesting was not reported and deemed not important. 11. Five trials were included in the analysis: three cluster randomized controlled trials (RCTs) (Rhodes, Young 2013, Young 2015), one individual RCT (Washington), and one stepped-wedge trial (Tang 2018). 12. The Rhodes study was the only one to compare social media interventions to no social media intervention. 13. Four RCTs (Young 2013, Young 2015, Tang 2018, Washington) used social media in both the intervention and control arms. 14. The Rhodes study had a high risk of bias due to recruitment bias and lack of blinding of participants and personnel. Other domains had unclear risks of bias, but there were no concerns about allocation concealment, baseline imbalance, or differential loss of clusters. 15. Consistency could not be assessed with only one study, leading to a downgrade in certainty. 16. Precision could not be assessed due to the lack of denominator data, resulting in another downgrade in certainty. 17. The GRADE assessment for website-based (non-social media) interventions was conducted by the same team of authors. 18. The primary question addressed was whether website-based interventions are effective in increasing the uptake of HIV testing and subsequent linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. 19. The certainty of evidence for the uptake of HIV testing was rated as very low. All five studies included heterogeneous website-based interventions, and none compared a website-based intervention to a control arm without a website-based component. 20. Linkage to care among individuals testing positive for HIV was not reported. 21. The number of new HIV-positive diagnoses was not reported. 22. The yield of HIV testing services (HTS) was not measured. 23. Viral suppression outcomes were not reported. 24. Linkage to prevention services was not reported. 25. The time to retesting was not reported and deemed not important. 26. Five individual RCTs were included: Bauermeister, Bull, Blas, Mikolajczak, and Tang 2016. 27. None of the studies compared a website-based intervention to a control without a website-based component, and no pooling of data was conducted. 28. The risk of bias assessment revealed high risks of bias in several studies: Bauermeister: High risk due to incomplete outcome data and unclear risk for other elements. Blas: High risk for blinding of participants and personnel, and unclear risk for other domains. Mikolajczak: High risk due to incomplete outcome data and unclear risk for other elements. Tang 2016: High risk related to allocation concealment, random sequence generation, and unclear blinding of outcome assessors. Bull: High risk due to lack of blinding, incomplete outcome data, and selective outcome reporting. 29. These studies did not experimentally assess the impact of website-based interventions on the uptake of HIV testing. 30. Tang 2016 reported yield but did not compare a website-based intervention to a non-website-based intervention (32% vs. 30%). 31. The GRADE assessment for SMS-based interventions was conducted by the same team of authors. 32. The primary question addressed was whether SMS interventions are effective in increasing the uptake of HIV testing and subsequent linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. 33. The certainty of evidence for the uptake of HIV testing was rated as moderate, with a pooled estimate showing no significant difference (0 fewer per 1,000, with a range from 1 fewer to 2 more). 34. Viral load outcomes among individuals testing positive were not reported. 35. Linkage to prevention services was not reported. 36. The time to retesting was not reported and deemed not important. 37. Eight trials were included: Mugo, de Tolly, Odeny, Wilson, Heerden, Kelvin 2018, Kelvin 2019, and Njuguna (cluster RCT). 38. Three studies with count data and SMS versus an unincentivized control were pooled (Mugo, de Tolly, Odeny). 39. Wilson included SMS in both the intervention and control arms. 40. Kelvin 2018 and Kelvin 2019 investigated the impact of three different types of SMS on testing uptake and yield but did not include a control arm without SMS. 41. Njuguna 2016 investigated SMS with different types of messages but did not include a control without SMS. 42. The risk of bias assessment revealed: Mugo: No serious issues except for the absence of blinding (participants, personnel, and outcome assessors). De Tolly: Incomplete outcome data and low external validity, with unclear risk for other elements. Odeny: High risk for incomplete outcome data and lack of blinding of participants and personnel, with unclear risk for blinding of outcome assessors. 43. Heterogeneity in effect size was explained by differences in intervention mechanisms (e.g., motivational vs. informational messages, varying message intensities) and population characteristics (e.g., parents of infants, high-risk adults, general adults). 44. The meta-analysis estimate was relatively precise and not downgraded. 45. Heerden had a high risk of bias for incomplete outcome data and unclear risk for other domains except allocation concealment. 46. Consistency could not be assessed with only one study, leading to a downgrade in certainty. 47. Pooled estimates were imprecise due to small denominators, resulting in a downgrade in certainty. 48. Odeny had incomplete outcome data and lacked blinding of participants and personnel, with unclear risk for blinding of outcome assessors. Outcomes were assessed on a subset of individuals who tested rather than the randomized denominator. 49. Mugo, Odeny, and Wilson were included in the pooled analysis. 50. The risk of bias assessment for Wilson revealed incomplete outcome data, with outcomes assessed on a subset of individuals who tested rather than the randomized denominator.
